blocks.prompt: The Flower That Drinks With Its Feet
blocks.text: A flower cannot walk to get a drink. It does not need to. Its roots spread out under the ground like fingers. They pull water out of the soil. The water goes up the stem. The stem is like a straw, and it holds the flower up so it does not fall over. At the top are the leaves. Leaves are flat and green. They catch sunlight and turn it into food for the plant. The petals are the bright part. Bees see the color from far away. They fly over to get a sweet drink called nectar. Every part has a job to do.

blocks.prompt: Four Parts, Four Jobs
blocks.text: Pick a flower out of the ground and you can see the whole plan at once. At the bottom are the roots. They do two jobs. They grip the soil so wind cannot tip the plant over, and they soak up water and the minerals dissolved in it. Next comes the stem. Inside it are tiny tubes, thinner than a hair, that carry that water all the way up. The stem also holds the leaves out where the light is. The leaves are the kitchen. They are flat and wide so they can catch as much sunlight as possible. Inside every leaf is a green stuff called chlorophyll, and chlorophyll uses sunlight to build sugar out of water and air. That sugar is the plant's food. It made its own lunch without moving. At the top are the petals. Petals do not feed the plant at all. They are a sign. Their bright color tells bees and butterflies that there is sweet nectar here. While an insect drinks, it gets dusted with pollen and carries it to the next flower. That is how the plant makes seeds. A flower is not made to be pretty. It is pretty because that works.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: The Four Parts, and What They Are Really Doing
blocks.text: Look at a flower from the side and you are looking at a machine with four working parts. Start underground. The roots are not just stakes holding the plant in place, though they do that too. Each root is covered in root hairs so fine you can barely see them, and they give the plant an enormous amount of surface to drink with. A single rye plant can grow hundreds of miles of root, and thousands more of root hair. The stem is plumbing. Inside it run two sets of pipes. One set, the xylem, carries water up from the roots. The xylem is made of cells that died on purpose: they hollow themselves out and stack end to end into an open pipe. The other set, the phloem, is alive, and it carries sugar from the leaves down to everything that cannot make its own. The leaves are the factory. The underside of a leaf is covered in thousands of tiny mouths called stomata, which open to let in air and close when the plant is drying out. Inside, chlorophyll catches sunlight and uses it to snap apart water and carbon dioxide and rebuild them as sugar. The leftover is oxygen, which the plant simply lets go. You are breathing it now. Then the petals, which do no work at all. Petals are leaves that gave up being green. Many of them carry patterns in ultraviolet light, invisible to you, that point straight at the nectar like runway lights. The bee sees the sign. It lands, drinks, picks up pollen, and carries it to the next flower without ever knowing it was hired.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Transpiration: water escaping a leaf pulls more up behind it
No pump, no heart, no muscle
Roots trade sugar with fungi for minerals
Petals are modified leaves
Nectar guides show up in ultraviolet light

blocks.prompt: The Pump That Is Not There
blocks.text: A flower has four visible parts, and each one is solving a problem you would struggle to solve yourself. Consider the water first. A sunflower can stand ten feet tall, and every drop of water in its highest leaf came from the soil at the bottom. There is no pump. The plant has no heart, no muscle, nothing that squeezes. So how does water climb? The answer starts at the top, not the bottom. On the underside of every leaf are thousands of adjustable pores called stomata. They open to let carbon dioxide in, and while they are open, water vapor escapes. That escape is called transpiration, and it is the engine. Water molecules cling to one another with surprising strength. As one molecule evaporates out of a leaf, it tugs the molecule behind it, which tugs the one behind that, and the pull travels down an unbroken thread of water through the xylem, all the way to the root hairs in the soil. The plant does not push water up. The sky pulls it up, and the plant just makes sure the thread never breaks. The roots hold the bottom of that thread. They also anchor the plant, and they trade with the soil: sugar leaks out of the roots to feed fungi, and the fungi hand back minerals the plant cannot reach on its own. It is an ancient deal, older than trees. The leaves spend the water they raised. Chlorophyll captures light and uses its energy to take apart water and carbon dioxide, then reassemble the pieces into sugar. Oxygen is the waste product, vented and forgotten. Almost every breath you take is a plant's exhaust. And the petals do nothing useful at all, which is exactly the point. Petals are modified leaves that traded chlorophyll for pigment. They cannot feed the plant. What they can do is advertise. Color, scent, and ultraviolet patterns invisible to human eyes all say the same thing to a passing bee: sweet nectar, this way. The bee comes for the nectar and leaves wearing pollen. The plant, which cannot walk, has just arranged its own delivery. Four parts. A rope of water, a set of pipes, a factory, and a billboard.

meta.templateLabel: The Flower That Drinks With Its Feet

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Van Helmont's willow: gained 164 pounds, the soil lost 2 ounces
Plant dry mass comes mostly from carbon dioxide
Cohesion and tension lift water with no pump
Xylem cells die on purpose to become pipes
Root and fungus partnerships are over 400 million years old
A petal is a leaf that traded chlorophyll for pigment

blocks.prompt: The Flower Is Mostly Made of Air
blocks.text: In the early 1600s, a Flemish physician named Jan Baptist van Helmont did something almost nobody had thought to do: he weighed a question. He dried out a quantity of soil, weighed it precisely at 200 pounds, packed it into a pot, planted a young willow shoot weighing five pounds, and covered the pot so nothing could blow in. For five years he added nothing but water. Then he pulled the tree out and weighed it again. The willow had gained roughly 164 pounds. The soil had lost about two ounces. Van Helmont drew the obvious conclusion and got it mostly wrong. He decided the tree was made of water. What he had actually done was prove a negative, and it was a good one: whatever a plant is built from, it is not dirt. The tree had not eaten the pot. So where did 164 pounds of willow come from? Look again at the four parts of a flower, and the answer is hiding in plain sight. The roots are the least impressive part of the story, which is surprising, because they are the part that looks like a mouth. Roots anchor the plant and pull in water and dissolved minerals. Those minerals matter enormously, but they are a trace ingredient, closer to vitamins than to food. Roots also run a trade: they leak sugar into the soil to feed fungal threads, and the fungi return phosphorus and nitrogen the plant could never reach alone. That partnership is older than trees themselves. The stem is infrastructure, and it solves a problem with no moving parts. Water has to climb, sometimes hundreds of feet, and the plant owns no pump. Instead, evaporation from the leaves does the lifting. Water leaving a leaf tugs on the water behind it, and because water molecules stick to each other stubbornly, the pull carries down an unbroken column through hollow xylem cells to the roots. The plant is not pushing. It is hanging a rope of water from the sky and holding on. The leaves are where van Helmont's missing pounds come from. Stomata on the underside of a leaf open, and carbon dioxide drifts in. Chlorophyll traps sunlight and spends that energy prying apart water and carbon dioxide, then bolting the carbon into chains of sugar. Oxygen is left over and released. Nearly all the dry weight of that willow, all 164 pounds of wood and bark and leaf, was assembled out of water and thin air, using light as the tool. The tree was, in the most literal sense, built out of sky. The petals contribute nothing to any of this, and that is the most interesting fact about them. A petal is a leaf that abandoned chlorophyll for pigment. It cannot feed the plant. Its entire function is persuasion. Color, scent, ultraviolet stripes that human eyes cannot see, and a bribe of sugar water at the base: every one of those is aimed at an animal that can do the one thing a plant cannot, which is move. The bee arrives for the nectar, blunders through the pollen, and delivers it to the next flower. The flower has outsourced its only impossible task. That is the whole machine. A rope of water, a set of pipes, a factory that eats light, and an advertisement. Van Helmont weighed the wrong thing and still moved science forward, because he proved that the answer was not in the pot. It took another 150 years to find the rest of it, and the rest of it was in the air the whole time.
